frictionVectors.title: European energy dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong state control over gas exports and uses pipeline and LNG relationships to preserve strategic autonomy. European buyers remain influential as Algeria seeks investment without surrendering control over upstream assets.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara and Sahel alignment
frictionVectors.details: Algiers faces diplomatic competition with Morocco and security spillover from the Sahel. Its support for regional sovereignty and non-intervention limits cooperation with some Western partners.

frictionVectors.title: External control of hydrocarbons
frictionVectors.details: Angola retains formal ownership of its oil resources, but production, technology, and financing remain heavily dependent on foreign operators and creditors. Declining output and debt-service needs constrain Luanda's bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito Corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: The rail corridor linking the Copperbelt to the Atlantic has become a focus of US, European, Chinese, and Gulf interest. Infrastructure investment could diversify Angola's economy, but competing external agendas risk limiting national control over strategic logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Cotonou corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Benin is strengthening the Port of Cotonou and regional trade links, but logistics, finance, and construction remain exposed to foreign operators and lenders. Revenue gains depend on maintaining access to neighboring markets.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel border insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Militant violence near the northern borders is increasing security costs and drawing external security assistance. Pressure from instability in Burkina Faso and Niger complicates Benin's effort to protect infrastructure and sovereign territory.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond-market concentration
frictionVectors.details: Botswana maintains unusually strong public oversight of diamond revenues, but its fiscal position remains exposed to global demand and the commercial power of major trading partners. Negotiations over beneficiation and marketing are central to preserving value domestically.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: New interest in copper, nickel, and other minerals creates opportunities to diversify beyond diamonds. Botswana must prevent foreign capital and infrastructure deals from reproducing enclave-style extraction.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector sovereignty drive
frictionVectors.details: The government is asserting greater control over industrial and artisanal gold production to capture more revenue and reduce reliance on foreign companies. Weak oversight and insecurity risk shifting extraction toward opaque networks rather than effective state control.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security partnership
frictionVectors.details: Ouagadougou is reducing dependence on France and regional institutions while relying more heavily on Russian-linked security support. This may increase regime autonomy in the short term but creates new external leverage and reputational costs.

frictionVectors.title: Border Security and Regional Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Burundi remains exposed to instability in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and tensions with Rwanda. Cross-border insecurity constrains trade and keeps national resources focused on defense.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Mineral Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, gold, and rare-mineral prospects attract foreign investors, but limited processing capacity leaves Burundi vulnerable to externally controlled value chains and weak bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: External Port and Connectivity Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde benefits from investment in ports, aviation, and digital infrastructure, but its small market and dependence on foreign financing limit autonomous control over strategic connectivity assets.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime Security Burden
frictionVectors.details: The archipelago remains vulnerable to illicit trafficking and illegal fishing across its large maritime zone. Enforcement depends substantially on European and wider international cooperation.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Commodity Chains
frictionVectors.details: Oil, gas, timber, and mining revenues remain exposed to foreign operators, opaque contracting, and limited domestic processing. The Kribi corridor increases export capacity but does not by itself ensure stronger national value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Separatist Conflict and Infrastructure Risk
frictionVectors.details: Violence in the Northwest and Southwest regions threatens roads, plantations, and public infrastructure while complicating resource governance. Cross-border insecurity also raises pressure on Cameroon’s security apparatus.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and Diamond Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups, foreign security actors, and informal networks compete for control of gold and diamonds. Weak state oversight allows external actors to capture substantial value while formal public revenues remain limited.

frictionVectors.title: Dependence on Russian Security Support
frictionVectors.details: Russian security personnel remain central to regime protection and military operations, creating deep political and resource-security dependence. This relationship can reduce short-term coup risk while narrowing Bangui’s strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Revenue and Foreign Operator Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chad’s fiscal and political system remains heavily dependent on oil exports and foreign technical, financial, and trading partners. Volatile prices and opaque revenue management limit sovereign control over national resource wealth.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Dependence and Sudan Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Chad’s security posture remains shaped by external military relationships and instability along the Sudanese border. Refugee flows, armed-group movement, and regional competition absorb state capacity and threaten transport corridors.

frictionVectors.title: France–Comoros territorial dispute
frictionVectors.details: Moroni continues to contest French control of Mayotte, while migration enforcement and maritime sovereignty remain recurring flashpoints.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Comoros relies heavily on remittances and external development partners, limiting policy autonomy over infrastructure and strategic sectors.

frictionVectors.title: M23–Rwanda security crisis
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in North and South Kivu continues to undermine state authority, displace civilians, and expose Kinshasa to regional and international pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral-sector bargaining pressure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain deeply embedded in copper and cobalt supply chains, while Western-backed initiatives seek alternative critical-minerals corridors and greater transparency.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on offshore oil leaves Brazzaville vulnerable to price shocks and gives foreign energy companies substantial influence over production and revenue flows.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed infrastructure and longstanding French commercial ties provide needed capital but constrain strategic autonomy through debt and contract dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of cocoa value chains
frictionVectors.details: Government efforts to raise farmer incomes and expand domestic processing are gradually improving sovereignty, but multinational traders still dominate financing and export channels.

frictionVectors.title: Port and security competition
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan is attracting major foreign infrastructure investment while balancing French, Chinese, Gulf, and regional interests amid insecurity spreading south from the Sahel.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military-base competition
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its position beside the Bab el-Mandeb through U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities, but this also exposes it to great-power rivalry.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed rail and port infrastructure has strengthened connectivity with Ethiopia while increasing concerns over debt exposure and external influence over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Suez Canal Security
frictionVectors.details: Red Sea and regional conflict risks continue to threaten shipping volumes and canal receipts. Egypt is balancing naval security, diplomatic mediation, and dependence on global trade flows it cannot fully control.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Leverage
frictionVectors.details: IMF programs, Gulf investment, and foreign asset sales provide liquidity but increase outside influence over strategic infrastructure, exchange-rate policy, and resource allocation.

frictionVectors.title: Declining Oil and Gas Output
frictionVectors.details: Maturing fields and weaker production are narrowing fiscal space, making the state more dependent on foreign operators, LNG partnerships, and new offshore exploration.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque Infrastructure Finance
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-linked construction and energy financing remain important to national infrastructure, while limited transparency complicates assessment of debt exposure and genuine domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects provide hard currency but leave Eritrea reliant on external capital, technical expertise, and export channels. Contract opacity and sanctions risk constrain sovereign bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Assab and Massawa sit within intense Red Sea competition involving Gulf states, Turkey, Ethiopia, and wider maritime powers. Security partnerships can generate leverage but also expose Eritrea to regional escalation.

frictionVectors.title: South African Economic Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Revenue from the Southern African Customs Union and supply chains linked to South Africa supports fiscal stability, but leaves Eswatini vulnerable to regional downturns and policy shifts.

frictionVectors.title: Investor Confidence and Governance
frictionVectors.details: Political tensions and governance concerns can deter infrastructure and manufacturing investment. External partners therefore retain significant influence over diversification prospects and financing conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Basin Tensions
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam strengthens Ethiopia's energy and bargaining position, but unresolved operating disputes with Egypt and Sudan remain a major regional security risk.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Infrastructure Finance
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and engagement with the IMF and international lenders can stabilize the economy while constraining policy autonomy. Chinese exposure to major infrastructure adds another layer of strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and Oil Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are seeking greater state participation and local processing in oil and manganese, creating tension with established foreign operators. Fiscal pressure may limit how aggressively contracts can be revised.

frictionVectors.title: Railway and Port Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gabon relies on foreign capital and expertise for the Transgabonese railway and export corridors. Disruptions would directly threaten manganese and timber revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Fisheries
frictionVectors.details: Limited monitoring capacity leaves Gambian waters vulnerable to illegal, underreported, and foreign fishing. This weakens food security and reduces the state's ability to capture marine-resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Banjul's trade and electricity systems depend heavily on external financing, regional links, and imported fuel. Senegalese connectivity is strategically valuable but also increases asymmetry in bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal Gold Mining
frictionVectors.details: Galamsey damages water systems, farmland, and state authority while creating openings for foreign-backed informal networks. Enforcement remains politically difficult because mining supports local livelihoods.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Mineral Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Ghana is seeking more local value addition and stronger state terms in gold and lithium while managing debt and IMF constraints. External investors retain substantial leverage over capital, technology, and export infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou Foreign Control
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore project promises major export revenues but depends on multinational consortia, Chinese participation, and large rail-and-port investments. Guinea's challenge is converting strategic leverage into durable domestic processing and public revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Bauxite exports remain concentrated in foreign-operated enclaves and logistics corridors. The junta's tougher contract posture increases state leverage but also raises investor and diplomatic friction.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew Value-Chain Capture
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains heavily dependent on raw cashew exports, with foreign traders and processors capturing much of the value. Weak regulation and political instability constrain domestic agro-processing.

frictionVectors.title: Fishing and Port Influence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing fleets and external actors retain significant influence over maritime resources and port development. Limited enforcement capacity leaves Guinea-Bissau vulnerable to revenue leakage and illicit trafficking.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: Kenya is diversifying financing and renegotiating major infrastructure obligations, but Chinese lending, construction contracts, and digital infrastructure remain significant sources of external leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Competition around Mombasa and regional transport corridors places pressure on Kenya to balance Gulf, Chinese, Western, and regional interests while protecting control of strategic logistics assets.

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Water exports to South Africa generate vital revenue but deepen structural dependence and expose Lesotho to disputes over pricing, construction delays, and control of long-term infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Economic dependence on South Africa
frictionVectors.details: South African markets, customs arrangements, finance, and employment opportunities dominate Lesotho's economic space, limiting autonomous resource and industrial policy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign mining concessions
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore and other mining projects offer fiscal upside but leave Liberia exposed to disputes over concession terms, local value addition, environmental safeguards, and revenue capture.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor control
frictionVectors.details: Foreign operators and investors remain central to Monrovia's port and mining-logistics infrastructure, creating recurring sovereignty concerns over tariffs, access, and strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Oil blockade and export vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed factions retain the ability to disrupt production and exports, turning Libya's hydrocarbons into a bargaining tool and weakening unified state control of national revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Competing external military influence
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia, and other regional actors maintain security and political leverage through rival Libyan networks, constraining sovereign decision-making and complicating infrastructure protection.

frictionVectors.title: Large-scale mining dependence
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mineral projects provide exports and infrastructure but expose Madagascar to foreign ownership, volatile commodity prices, and disputes over taxation and environmental costs.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic coastline and maritime access
frictionVectors.details: Madagascar's ports, fisheries, and Indian Ocean position attract competing Gulf, Asian, and Western interests, while limited state capacity hampers enforcement of maritime and resource sovereignty.

highlights: Debt restructuring opens room for mining-led recovery
Fuel and foreign-exchange shortages remain binding

frictionVectors.title: Mining concessions and fiscal leverage
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is courting foreign capital for uranium, rare earths and other minerals while debt-relief conditions constrain its bargaining space. Weak regulatory capacity creates risks of low state capture of future resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: Import-dependent infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Fuel, fertilizer and electricity supply remain vulnerable to foreign-exchange shortages and external financing delays. Transport and power bottlenecks limit Malawi's ability to monetize resources independently.

highlights: Junta prioritizes gold sovereignty and strategic autonomy
Russian security dependence deepens amid regional isolation

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are seeking a larger state share and tighter control over industrial gold operations, increasing friction with foreign mining companies. Contract uncertainty and insecurity could reduce investment without guaranteeing stronger public revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security footprint
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian military assistance provides regime protection but creates opaque financial and political obligations. It also complicates relations with Western partners and regional neighbors while insecurity continues to disrupt transport and production.

highlights: Iron and fisheries remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: GTA gas dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project strengthens Mauritania's bargaining position but leaves early gas revenues and technical operations dependent on international partners. Revenue management and local-content rules will determine whether the project builds durable sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Port and mining corridors
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed rail, port and iron-ore infrastructure is essential to Mauritania's export model. Concentrated dependence on external operators and commodity markets limits domestic control over logistics and value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos transition management
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius has gained greater political leverage over the Chagos issue, but implementation, security arrangements and the future of Diego Garcia remain sensitive. Managing relations with the United Kingdom, United States and India will test sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: External capital concentration
frictionVectors.details: The financial, tourism and offshore sectors remain highly exposed to foreign investors and global tax-policy changes. This creates influence risks even as Mauritius retains strong institutions and diversified diplomatic partnerships.

highlights: Phosphate and green-energy strategy reinforce state leverage
Western Sahara remains the central sovereignty contest

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara resource diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco uses phosphate, fisheries and renewable-energy projects to consolidate control and attract international recognition of its position. The strategy continues to generate legal and diplomatic friction with Algeria, the Polisario Front and some European stakeholders.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign dependence in strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Major rail, port, automotive and renewable projects rely on European, Gulf and Chinese capital and technology. Rabat retains substantial policy control, but external financing can shape industrial priorities and supply-chain exposure.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent activity continues to constrain state authority and delay the full development of offshore gas projects. Mozambique relies heavily on foreign security support, including Rwanda and regional partners.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign LNG dominance
frictionVectors.details: International energy companies and lenders control much of the capital, technology, and marketing capacity surrounding Mozambique's gas sector, limiting near-term domestic value capture.

highlights: Oil and green hydrogen reshape strategy

frictionVectors.title: Offshore oil ownership
frictionVectors.details: Recent offshore discoveries could transform state revenues, but foreign operators retain the technology and financing needed to commercialize them. Windfall expectations are increasing pressure for stronger local-content and fiscal terms.

frictionVectors.title: External control of green infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: European and Gulf-backed investment is accelerating green-hydrogen and port projects, creating opportunities while raising concerns about land, water, export infrastructure, and long-term value retention.

highlights: Oil and uranium face transport constraints

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and export dependence
frictionVectors.details: Niger seeks greater control over oil and uranium assets, but export routes, technical capacity, and financing remain dependent on neighboring states and external firms. Disputes with operators and transit partners threaten revenue stability.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel security realignment
frictionVectors.details: The junta's break with France and closer ties to Russia and the Alliance of Sahel States have increased strategic autonomy but reduced access to some Western finance, intelligence, and development infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Upstream investment and production losses
frictionVectors.details: International oil companies remain central to capital-intensive production, while theft, sabotage, and regulatory uncertainty weaken Nigeria's ability to capture full value from its reserves.

frictionVectors.title: Critical infrastructure insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Pipeline vandalism, organized theft, and attacks in the Niger Delta continue to undermine state control over energy infrastructure. Refining expansion improves leverage but does not yet eliminate dependence on imported inputs and foreign technology.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo resource allegations
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's security posture and alleged support for armed actors in eastern DRC generate sustained diplomatic pressure over mineral flows and regional sovereignty. Sanctions risk and border escalation could constrain Kigali's economic diplomacy.

frictionVectors.title: External aid and investment leverage
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda retains strong state control over strategic projects, but development finance, technology, and major investment remain linked to Western, Gulf, and multilateral partners. This creates exposure when security or governance disputes trigger conditionality.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore exploration dependence
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon prospects remain commercially uncertain, while foreign operators and licensing partners would control much of any future development. Weak state capacity limits São Tomé and Príncipe's leverage over contracts and revenues.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: Portugal, China, and other partners compete for influence through port, telecommunications, and public-sector projects. The country generally preserves diplomatic flexibility but remains vulnerable to debt and project-finance dependence.

highlights: First oil and gas revenues reshape leverage

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon contract renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: New offshore production offers Senegal greater fiscal room, but disputes over contract terms, local content, and revenue transparency could strain relations with foreign operators and lenders.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics competition
frictionVectors.details: Dakar's role as a regional hub faces competition from ports in Mauritania, Côte d'Ivoire, and Morocco. Chinese, Gulf, European, and Turkish infrastructure interests create opportunities while increasing external influence over strategic corridors.

highlights: Blue economy remains the sovereignty strategy

frictionVectors.title: Maritime security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles relies on India, France, the United States, and other partners for maritime surveillance and anti-piracy support across its vast EEZ. This strengthens security but constrains fully independent control of maritime operations.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: Port modernization and tourism infrastructure attract competing foreign capital, especially from India, China, and Gulf states. The government must balance investment needs against strategic dependence and environmental limits.

highlights: Mining drives growth but limits bargaining power

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore and mineral concentration
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-controlled mining remains central to exports and fiscal prospects, leaving Sierra Leone exposed to commodity cycles and uneven value capture. Local processing and stronger contract enforcement remain difficult goals.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms and financing remain important in roads, construction, and resource-linked infrastructure. These projects expand state capacity but can deepen repayment risks and reduce negotiating room if revenues weaken.

highlights: Maritime sovereignty becomes a national priority

frictionVectors.title: Offshore resource competition
frictionVectors.details: Prospective oil and gas development is entangled with federal-state disputes, weak regulatory capacity, and competing foreign interests. Without a durable revenue-sharing framework, exploration could intensify internal fragmentation rather than strengthen sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign security and port influence
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, the Gulf states, the United States, and other partners provide security or port-related support, often tied to strategic access. These arrangements help contain threats but leave Somalia dependent on external actors for control of critical infrastructure and waters.

frictionVectors.title: GRID AND PORT BOTTLENECKS
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages, rail failures, and port congestion limit South Africa’s ability to control and monetize its mineral supply chains. State capacity is being supplemented by private operators and external capital.

frictionVectors.title: MINERALS COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: The United States, European powers, and China are competing for influence over platinum-group metals, manganese, and other strategic minerals, creating pressure for Pretoria to balance nonalignment with investment needs.

frictionVectors.title: OIL TRANSIT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan’s crude exports depend on infrastructure crossing Sudan, leaving revenue and national sovereignty exposed to Sudan’s war, pipeline disruptions, and bargaining by external operators.

frictionVectors.title: REGIONAL SECURITY LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Uganda, Sudan, Kenya, and other regional actors retain significant security and political influence as internal power-sharing remains incomplete and armed factions compete for control of oil-producing areas.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD AND ARMED FINANCE
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling remain central to financing rival armed networks, with foreign buyers and regional intermediaries benefiting from weak state oversight.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND PIPELINE VULNERABILITY
frictionVectors.details: The conflict threatens Port Sudan, oil-export infrastructure, and humanitarian supply routes, giving external states leverage over Sudan’s remaining commercial and logistical lifelines.

highlights: LNG and corridor projects regain momentum

frictionVectors.title: LNG CONTRACT LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is seeking major gas investment while attempting to preserve fiscal and regulatory control, creating tensions over project terms, local content, and export destinations.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND RAIL INFLUENCE
frictionVectors.details: Competition among Gulf, Chinese, Turkish, and Western investors around Dar es Salaam and regional transport corridors could expand capacity while increasing foreign leverage over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: PORT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Lomé’s importance as a West African transshipment and logistics hub attracts substantial foreign commercial influence, while regional insecurity raises the cost of protecting trade routes.

frictionVectors.title: PHOSPHATE VALUE CHAIN
frictionVectors.details: Togo retains strategic phosphate reserves but relies on external finance, technology, and markets, limiting the state’s ability to capture the full value of downstream processing.

frictionVectors.title: Migration Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: European funding and political engagement remain closely tied to Tunisia's cooperation on migration control, limiting room for fully independent policy. Domestic criticism frames the arrangement as externalized border management.

frictionVectors.title: Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains exposed to imported hydrocarbons and electricity constraints, while delayed investment in renewables and infrastructure increases vulnerability to external suppliers and financing conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Sanctions Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline continues to face criticism and legal pressure from Western governments and environmental groups, complicating financing, insurance, and project diplomacy.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese contractors and lenders remain important to Uganda's transport and energy build-out, creating useful alternatives to Western capital but increasing long-term exposure to concentrated external financing.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt demand has intensified competition among Chinese, Western, and Gulf investors, giving Zambia leverage while risking renewed dependence on foreign operators and commodity-price cycles.

frictionVectors.title: Power Supply Bottleneck
frictionVectors.details: Drought-driven electricity shortages have constrained mines and industry, forcing Zambia to rely more heavily on imports and emergency investment while exposing weaknesses in domestic energy resilience.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Zimbabwe is seeking greater local processing and state oversight of lithium, platinum, and other minerals, but Chinese and other foreign investors retain substantial influence over capital, technology, and market access.

frictionVectors.title: External Finance Isolation
frictionVectors.details: Sanctions, arrears, and limited access to international finance push Harare toward narrower partnerships, increasing dependence on politically aligned investors and commodity-backed arrangements.
